item_name: Steering Actuation Approaches for Formula Student Driverless
competition_series: Applies across FSG, FSAE (incl. FSAE-A), FS UK, FS Czech, FS East and other FSAE-derived driverless rulesets - all require an autonomous steering actuator satisfying an equivalent of DT.2.1 (manual steering preservation) and DT.2.2 (actuator decoupling).
summary: Across the Formula Student driverless corpus reviewed (Politecnico di Torino/Squadra Corse theses on an electromechanical actuator and a separate Electric Power Steering system, the Chalmers bachelor's thesis documenting an early pneumatic-clamp linear actuator, and current OpenELAB guidance on integrated quasi-direct-drive actuators), steering actuation designs converge on a small set of architectures: a BLDC motor driving a ball screw either inline with the rack or via a planetary gearbox and belt/chain stage, a rack-parallel ball screw mounted directly at the rack, a linear actuator engaging the rack through a pneumatic clamp, or an increasingly common commercial-off-the-shelf integrated quasi-direct-drive (QDD) motor-gearbox-encoder module. The dominant design driver is DT.2.2 (actuator decoupling): back-drivable mechanisms (ball screws, low-reduction QDD units) let teams avoid designing a dedicated mechanical clutch, while higher-reduction gear/belt drives need an explicit disconnect. Static steering torque requirements are consistently derived from tie-rod/scrub-radius geometry and land in the roughly 7-20 Nm range depending on safety factor and dynamic tire-slip assumptions, with target lock-to-lock times around 0.4-0.9 s across the corpus. Component-level cost and lead-time data are thin: only one thesis (Politecnico di Torino, 18713) directly asks 'how much does it cost' and explicitly declines to answer, stating the cost of the proposed solution was out of scope; most other sources describe the engineering without disclosing sourcing cost. Emergency brake system (EBS) content is covered fully in a companion item and only summarized here.
evidence_quality: moderate: strong primary-source detail (multiple full master's/bachelor's theses with real torque calculations, motor selections, and documented bench-test failure modes) exists for steering actuator mechanical architecture and control approach, mainly from Politecnico di Torino/Squadra Corse and Chalmers; but cross-team aggregation of cost, procurement lead time, iteration count, and development duration is thin - one thesis explicitly declines to disclose cost, and most other teams referenced in this project's broader research (EUFS, Monash, e-gnition, TUfast, DUT, UTFR per prior research passes) do not publish steering-actuator-specific cost or duration figures at all, so those figures here are synthesized/estimated and flagged [uncertain].
months_concept_to_first_autonomous_run: [uncertain] Repurposed as: typical months from steering-actuator concept to a bench-validated actuator (commanded-vs-actual angle verified on a rig, not yet vehicle-integrated). Evidence: the Politecnico di Torino steering actuator thesis (18713) covers concept, three candidate-solution trade studies, and detailed sizing/selection of the winning ball-screw solution within roughly one academic year (2020-2021), explicitly stopping at 3D-printed-component interference-checking as its 'way forward' rather than a bench-tested build; the companion EPS thesis (16285) covers concept through a Simulink-validated control model within a similar academic-year timeframe. Estimated 6-9 months concept-to-bench-validated, similar to the EBS figure in the companion item, though sample size is very small.
months_concept_to_first_competition: [uncertain] Repurposed as: typical months from steering-actuator concept to a first competition attempt. No clean single-team figure was found. The Chalmers case is the most informative proxy: their initial pneumatic-clamp linear actuator was already in service for at least one competition season by the time the 2019 bachelor's thesis analyzed its play/backlash defect, and the thesis's own recommendation (redesign to a motor+pinion rack-and-pinion system) implies a second, longer design cycle would be needed to reach a competition-ready replacement - suggesting the realistic concept-to-competition timeline, INCLUDING at least one redesign iteration, commonly exceeds 12 months.
months_to_first_scoring_run: [uncertain] Repurposed as: typical months from steering-actuator concept to first scored autonomous dynamic event. No team in this corpus published this figure directly. Adjacent evidence from this project's broader team-level research (cited here for context, not primary to this item): AMZ's front-axle-mounted steering actuator achieves sub-0.9 s lock-to-lock while retaining the manual rack, implying a mature multi-year iteration (AMZ is one of the most established driverless programs in the sport); QUT's dedicated steering_actuator ROS2 node was first implemented Dec 2021, refactored Oct-Nov 2022, and still being re-tuned from telemetry as late as Nov 2024 - a roughly 3-year maturation arc from first implementation to stable competition tuning. Best estimate: 12-24 months to a first scored run with an actuator design that still needs further tuning, consistent with the EBS-item estimate for the parallel subsystem.

year_by_year_timeline.mechanical_focus: Derive static steering torque from tie-rod offset, scrub radius, and tire/road friction; add a safety factor (documented example: 1.5x) and a dynamic-condition multiplier for higher lateral-force cases (documented example: torque roughly doubling from ~9.9 Nm static to ~18.15 Nm dynamic).
year_by_year_timeline.electrical_focus: Decide motor class (BLDC rotary + gearbox/ball-screw vs. integrated QDD module) based on required continuous torque/speed envelope, not peak torque alone.
year_by_year_timeline.software_focus: Define the control-loop architecture (position vs. torque mode) and redundancy/feedback strategy (single vs. dual encoder).
year_by_year_timeline.milestone_achieved: Torque/speed specification and 2-3 candidate architecture concepts scored against design complexity, manufacturing lead time, and cost (documented example: a formal trade study comparing an inline ball-screw solution against a planetary-gearbox-plus-belt-drive solution).

year_by_year_timeline.mechanical_focus: CAD the chosen transmission (ball screw, belt, or QDD mount); verify DT.2.2 decoupling mechanism (clutch, pneumatic clamp, or back-drivable-by-design) works in both locked positions without removing parts.
year_by_year_timeline.electrical_focus: Select and procure the motor/gearbox/ball-screw or QDD module (documented example motor selection: a BLDC motor with a rated torque well above the calculated static requirement, coupled through a planetary gearbox to a ball screw).
year_by_year_timeline.software_focus: Model motor resisting torque/self-aligning moment in simulation (documented example: a Simulink model of motor resistant torque due to self-aligning moment) to validate the control law before hardware exists.
year_by_year_timeline.milestone_achieved: Completed detail CAD of the winning architecture; simulation-validated control model.

year_by_year_timeline.mechanical_focus: Fabricate/assemble the actuator and mounting; check for interferences with neighboring components (documented next-step: 3D-print components to check cockpit-space interference before final machining).
year_by_year_timeline.electrical_focus: Instrument the actuator and rack with redundant potentiometers/encoders for closed-loop feedback and diagnostics.
year_by_year_timeline.software_focus: Bench-test by comparing sent steering requests against potentiometer/encoder readings at both the actuator and the rack (the method that surfaced a documented backlash/play defect in one team's design).
year_by_year_timeline.milestone_achieved: Bench-validated commanded-vs-actual steering angle response; identification of any coupling backlash/play requiring redesign.

year_by_year_timeline.mechanical_focus: Install on vehicle; verify manual steering remains possible with the DSMS off (DT.2.1.1) and the decoupling mechanism operates correctly in both positions.
year_by_year_timeline.electrical_focus: Integrate actuator power supply so it is directly controlled by the DSMS/ASMS per the FSG reference guide's steering-safety precautions.
year_by_year_timeline.software_focus: Progressive on-vehicle testing at restricted speed, then full-speed autonomous testing; re-tune from live telemetry (documented pattern: at least one team re-tuned its steering actuator control from telemetry roughly a year after first implementation).
year_by_year_timeline.milestone_achieved: First on-vehicle autonomous steering; iteration toward a competition-stable tuning.

ramp_phases: Named phases observed/synthesized across sources: (1) 'Torque/speed sizing & architecture selection' 2-4 weeks; (2) 'Detail design & component selection', including a formal multi-criteria trade study between candidate architectures in at least one documented case, 4-8 weeks; (3) 'Procurement', gated by premium industrial motor/ball-screw lead times, 4-8 weeks, often parallel with (2); (4) 'Fabrication & assembly' 4-6 weeks; (5) 'Bench validation' (commanded-vs-actual angle testing at both actuator and rack) 2-4 weeks; (6) 'Vehicle integration & DT.2.2 decoupling verification' 4-8 weeks; (7) 'Progressive dynamic testing & re-tuning', open-ended, with at least one documented case still re-tuning from telemetry roughly a year after first implementation.
what_slipped: Common steering-actuator-specific slips/gaps found in this corpus: (1) Chalmers' original pneumatic-clamp linear actuator design was found, only after a season of use, to have play in the clamp causing quantified 'steering reduction' (commanded angle not fully achieved), worse on rough surfaces - a defect not caught in earlier development and requiring the team's own thesis to recommend a full redesign to a motor+pinion rack-and-pinion system; (2) the Politecnico di Torino steering actuator thesis (18713) completed a full architecture trade study and detailed design of the winning ball-screw solution but explicitly stopped before fabrication/bench-testing, deferring that to a later cycle - the same design-phase-consumes-all-available-time pattern seen in the companion EBS thesis; (3) the same thesis explicitly could not answer its own research question on cost ('the cost of developing the proposed solution is not covered in this thesis'), meaning cost estimation itself was descoped rather than completed; (4) QUT's steering_actuator node (per this project's broader team research) needed re-tuning from live telemetry roughly a year after first implementation, and was moved onto a different CAN translation path nearly three years after first implementation - indicating steering-actuator software tuning is a multi-year, not single-season, process even after the mechanical actuator itself is finished.
platform_prerequisites: N/A as a team-history field, but functionally significant: every steering actuator design in this corpus is engineered as an ADD-ON to a pre-existing manual rack-and-pinion (or equivalent) steering system, never as a replacement for it - DT.2.1.1 (manual steering must remain possible with the DSMS off) makes a working manual steering system a hard prerequisite, and every documented actuator (ball screw, belt drive, pneumatic clamp, QDD module) is designed to sit alongside or clamp onto the existing rack/column rather than modify the fundamental manual steering geometry.
ebs_design: Full detail is in the companion item 'Emergency Brake System (EBS) Design Approaches'. Summary: three architectures recur - direct pneumatic actuation of the existing hydraulic brake pedal/master cylinder via a compressed-air/CO2 cylinder and 3/2 solenoid valve; a pneumo-hydraulic intensifier hybrid where a certified compressed-air tank drives a custom intensifier producing 40-70 bar hydraulic pressure into duplicated brake lines (the most fully documented approach, from Politecnico di Torino/Squadra Corse); and an electromechanical spring-based 'removal of counterforce' design described in the official FSG reference guide but not found fully implemented in any thesis reviewed. All three satisfy DT.3.2.1.a (passive mechanical energy storage only) and duplicate hardware end-to-end to satisfy DT.3.2.5.c (half performance on single failure).

ebs_cost_estimate: See companion item 'Emergency Brake System (EBS) Design Approaches' for full detail; not the focus of this item.
steering_actuation:
Architectures documented, with concrete numbers where sourced:

1) BLDC MOTOR + PLANETARY GEARBOX + INLINE BALL SCREW (Politecnico di Torino/Squadra Corse SC19, chosen solution in thesis 18713): a BLDC motor (documented example motor: a Maxon unit) is rigidly coupled through a shaft coupling to a ball screw shaft (documented example: Bosch Rexroth ball screw with an adjustable-preload single nut); the ball screw's low friction and lack of self-retention allows manual back-driving when the motor is unpowered/decoupled, simplifying DT.2.2 compliance. Static steering torque was calculated from tie-rod geometry: friction torque on one wheel from lateral force x scrub radius = 6.17 Nm at the wheel, converting through the tie-rod offset (51.3 mm) and pinion radius (27.5 mm) to 6.62 Nm static torque at the pinion; applying a 1.5x safety factor gives 9.9 Nm required static torque, rising to roughly 18.15 Nm in a higher-lateral-force dynamic case (mu_y up to 1.65). Target: 30 rpm continuous rotary rate (or equivalently ~42.5-45 mm/s of rack linear travel).

2) BLDC MOTOR + PLANETARY GEARBOX + SYNCHRONOUS BELT DRIVE (Politecnico di Torino, 'Solution 2' - evaluated but not selected in thesis 18713): a toothed synchronous belt runs from the gearbox output to a pulley on the steering column, offering compact/flexible placement versus a coaxial ball-screw layout but requiring belt-tension management and adding a non-negligible backlash/compliance path; chain drive was ruled out early for similar reasons. Belts are explicitly permitted for autonomous steering actuators under the 2026 FSAE rules (a specific carve-out from the general prohibition on cable/belt actuation for the primary driver steering system, per rule text referencing T2.6.1-equivalent language).

3) RACK-PARALLEL BALL SCREW DRIVEN BY A BRUSHLESS SERVO MOTOR MOUNTED DIRECTLY AT THE RACK (pattern identified across several teams in this project's broader research, e.g. Chalmers' later design, Monash, EUFS): coupled to the rack via a cross-bore and shoulder screw; documented performance figures: full lock-to-lock steering in 0.4 seconds, ~2000 N at the rack with the car stationary, matching a human driver's performance roughly 99% of the time versus prior telemetry. The ball screw's low friction and lack of self-retention again allows manual driver steering once the actuator is decoupled; removable via a small bolt pattern (documented example: eight bolts plus the shoulder screw) in at least one case.

4) LINEAR ACTUATOR ENGAGING VIA A PNEUMATIC CLAMP, ORTHOGONAL TO THE STEERING COLUMN (Chalmers' original 2018-2019 design): the linear actuator pushes the steering rack when clamped; the clamp opens to allow manual steering when autonomous steering is disengaged, and the actuator must move to line up with the rack and then clamp to engage. DOCUMENTED FAILURE MODE: measurable play in the clamp caused 'steering reduction' - the rack does not reach the fully commanded angle - confirmed by comparing sent steering requests against potentiometer readings at both the actuator and the rack; the effect was worse on rougher track surfaces. The team's own thesis conclusion recommended redesigning to a motor-and-pinion rack-and-pinion system instead, specifically to eliminate the clamp/backlash path entirely.

5) FRONT-AXLE-MOUNTED ROTARY ACTUATOR (AMZ, per this project's broader team research): a motor mounted under the front axle, capable of moving full-lock-left to full-lock-right in under 0.9 s, with the manual steering rack retained for DT.2.1.1 compliance; specific motor model/gearing not disclosed in the sources available to this project.

6) INTEGRATED QUASI-DIRECT-DRIVE (QDD) ACTUATOR MODULES (current/emerging approach per OpenELAB 2026 guidance, not confirmed as implemented by any specific team in the primary sources reviewed): commercial integrated motor-gearbox-dual-encoder units eliminate a separate gearbox/coupling stage. Two example candidate models compared: CubeMars AK10-9 V3.0 (18 Nm continuous / 53 Nm peak torque, 235 rpm, 940 g, dual encoder) and AK80-9 V3.0 (9 Nm continuous / 22 Nm peak, 390 rpm, 490 g, single encoder). Guidance stresses sizing on CONTINUOUS duty-cycle torque, not peak, and warns that actuator-side encoder precision does not guarantee vehicle-level angle accuracy since backlash/compliance can occur downstream in the belt, coupling, rack joint, or tire deflection - directly echoing the Chalmers clamp-play failure mode above.
brake_actuation: See companion item 'Emergency Brake System (EBS) Design Approaches' for full detail on service/EBS brake actuation; not the focus of this item.
sensor_mounting_packaging: Steering-actuator-specific packaging notes: DT.2.3 requires all Driverless System components (including the actuator's control electronics) to sit inside the defined chassis/tire volume or permitted aerodynamic-device zones. The FSG reference guide's steering-system safety precautions add: the actuator supply must be directly controlled by the DSMS/ASMS; the system must not perform any steering actuation that would move the rack while the vehicle is not Ready-to-Drive (an exception is allowed, not required, to continue steering during an active Emergency Brake Maneuver while the vehicle is still moving, per DT.2.1.3); and no sensor or electrical component may contact the driver's helmet, typically checked with the tallest driver during technical inspection - a constraint that most directly affects where the actuator's control box/electronics can be mounted near the cockpit.
mass_added: [uncertain] No team in this corpus published a steering-actuator-only mass-added figure. Order-of-magnitude estimate synthesized from the component classes identified (motor, gearbox/ball-screw or QDD module, mounting bracket, decoupling mechanism): roughly 2-5 kg for a motor+gearbox+ball-screw or belt-drive assembly; a single integrated QDD module (e.g. the CubeMars AK-series examples above, at 490-940 g for the bare actuator) would add somewhat less mass at the actuator itself but still requires a mounting bracket and coupling hardware. This is a synthesized estimate, not a sourced figure - see the companion EBS item's mass_added field for the combined EBS+steering estimate used elsewhere in this project's research.
chassis_impact: Documented/typical impacts: the steering column or rack requires a new mounting bracket/interface for whichever actuator architecture is chosen (inline ball screw, off-axis belt drive, rack-parallel ball screw, or pneumatic-clamp linear actuator); at least one team (Chalmers) found its original coupling approach required a full redesign after in-service play/backlash was discovered, meaning chassis/mounting impact was not fully known until after a season of real driving; DT.2.2's requirement that the decoupling mechanism be 'securely locked in the two positions' without removing parts constrains bracket/mount design to accommodate an integrated, non-removable disconnect feature (clutch or back-drivable coupling) rather than a simple unbolt-and-remove interface.
compute_platform: N/A as a general compute-platform field for this item. Relevant detail: the steering control loop commonly runs on a dedicated motor controller rather than the main autonomy compute stack - the closest documented example (Politecnico di Torino EPS thesis, power-assist rather than full autonomous actuation) uses a Cyclic Synchronous Torque control mode on the motor controller, with the target trajectory computed upstream and only the torque-tracking loop running locally on the drive.
sensor_suite: Steering-actuator-relevant sensors identified: dual potentiometers/encoders, one at the actuator and one at the steering rack, for redundant, cross-checked angle feedback - the method used in the Chalmers thesis to diagnose the clamp-play defect by comparing sent steering requests to both readings; single vs. dual encoder is also a distinguishing spec between candidate COTS QDD actuator modules (documented example: the CubeMars AK10-9 V3.0 has dual encoders, the AK80-9 V3.0 has a single encoder), with dual-encoder designs offering better fault detection at the actuator itself, though OpenELAB's guidance stresses that actuator-level encoder precision alone does not guarantee vehicle-level (rack/wheel) angle accuracy.
power_budget: [uncertain] No team published a steering-actuator-specific power-draw figure for a full autonomous actuator. The closest sourced figure is from an EPS (driver power-assist, not full autonomous actuation) design using a Maxon EC 60 Flat motor rated at 150 W continuous, 3210 rpm nominal speed, 234 mNm nominal torque, with a torque constant of 52.5 mN*m/A - useful as an order-of-magnitude reference but likely an UNDER-estimate for a full autonomous actuator sized for the entire lock-to-lock steering authority (roughly 9.9-18.15 Nm at the pinion per the torque calculations documented above) rather than driver-assist torque alone.
shutdown_circuit_implementation: Per the FSG reference guide's steering-safety section: the steering actuator's power supply (or its power stages) must be directly controlled by the DSMS/ASMS, distinct from the general Shutdown Circuit relay chain documented for the EBS (see companion item). This directly protects the driver from an unintended steering actuation by the autonomous system during manual driving, since the actuator is simply unpowered whenever the DSMS is off.
remote_stop_system: Not steering-specific; see the companion EBS item for full Remote Stop System detail. One steering-relevant rule interaction: DT.2.1.3 explicitly allows (but does not require) the steering system to remain active during an Emergency Brake Maneuver while the vehicle is still moving, to help maintain a stable driving condition even after the EBS/Remote Stop has triggered - i.e. a Remote Stop trigger does not necessarily have to cut steering authority immediately.

control_approach: The most detailed documented control approach (Politecnico di Torino EPS thesis, power-assist context) uses a Cyclic Synchronous Torque (CST) control mode on the motor drive, with a Simulink model of the motor/mechanism dynamics (electromagnetic motor torque, resisting friction torque from tire/road contact, and self-aligning moment) used to validate the control law before hardware testing; the model uses the motor's torque constant (documented example: kt = 52.5 mN*m/A) and a damping coefficient derived from no-load torque/speed to characterize dynamics. The general industrial pattern noted for cost-effectiveness is a PID-based position/torque loop. Validation methodology across sources is empirical rather than purely simulation-based: the Chalmers thesis validated the real actuator by directly comparing a timestamped steering-angle REQUEST signal (range -25 deg to +25 deg documented) against POTENTIOMETER READINGS at both the linear actuator and the steering rack, which is how the clamp-backlash 'steering reduction' defect was identified and quantified - a bench/telemetry validation method rather than a pure control-theory approach.
simulation_tooling: Simulink was used in at least one documented case (Politecnico di Torino EPS thesis) to model motor resisting-torque and self-aligning-moment behavior and validate a linearized control law with computed gear ratios before physical testing. No dedicated multi-body or full-vehicle steering simulator (e.g. a CARLA/Gazebo-class tool) was cited by name for steering-actuator-specific validation in any source reviewed for this item; validation in practice relied primarily on direct commanded-vs-measured signal comparison (see control_approach) rather than simulation.
ci_cd_testing: N/A - not documented for this hardware subsystem in the sources reviewed; see validation_strategy for the bench/vehicle test sequence actually used.
data_logging: The most concrete documented data-logging use for steering validation is the direct time-series comparison of the sent steering-angle request against potentiometer readings at both the actuator and the rack (Chalmers thesis), plotted over time to characterize signal delay, actuation time, and steering-angle reduction under different conditions (documented: comparisons run on both smooth and rough track surfaces). The general FSAE Driverless Systems Form CAN DBC requirement (DSF.8, shared with the EBS/RES signal set described in the companion item) would also cover steering-actuator CAN signals where applicable, though no source gives steering-specific DBC detail.
open_source_repos: [uncertain] None of the primary theses/reference sources reviewed for this item are themselves public code repositories. One adjacent example from this project's broader team research (QUT Motorsport) is reported to maintain a dedicated 'steering_actuator' ROS2 package (CAN-based node relating target steering angle to actuator rotations, with encoder feedback) in a public GitHub org, but the exact repository URL was not captured in this research pass and is not re-cited here to avoid an unverified link.
critical_path_items: Top 3 across sources: (1) accurately deriving static AND dynamic steering torque from tie-rod/scrub-radius geometry with an appropriate safety factor - undersizing here (or sizing only from a peak-torque datasheet number rather than continuous duty-cycle capability, per OpenELAB's explicit warning) risks an actuator that cannot maintain commanded angle under real lateral load, which is exactly the failure mode documented at Chalmers; (2) selecting and validating the DT.2.2 decoupling mechanism (clutch vs. pneumatic clamp vs. inherently back-drivable ball screw/QDD) - the one mechanism in this corpus with a documented in-service failure (Chalmers' clamp) was also the one requiring active engagement/alignment logic, versus the passively back-drivable ball-screw designs which reported no equivalent defect; (3) bench-validating commanded-vs-actual angle response (via dual potentiometers/encoders at the actuator and the rack) BEFORE vehicle mounting - the corpus shows this step is what actually surfaces coupling backlash/play defects, and skipping or shortening it is explicitly called out as a mistake in current guidance (OpenELAB: 'skipping loaded bench testing... free-moving tests miss friction, compliance, and alignment errors').
long_lead_procurement: [uncertain] No source gives a directly-measured procurement lead time in weeks; the following are inferred from component class/sourcing channel and should be treated as estimates only: premium industrial BLDC motors and precision ball screws (documented example brands: Maxon, Bosch Rexroth) - est. 4-8 weeks as catalog-but-made-to-order industrial items, consistent with one thesis's own trade-study criteria explicitly listing 'manufacturing lead time' as a factor distinguishing candidate solutions; COTS integrated QDD actuator modules (e.g. CubeMars AK-series) - est. 1-3 weeks domestically, longer if shipped internationally from the primary Chinese suppliers; custom-machined mounting brackets/couplings and any custom pneumatic-clamp hardware - est. 2-4 weeks if using an in-house/university machine shop, longer if outsourced.

testing_hours_before_first_comp: [uncertain] No aggregate testing-hours figure was found for steering actuator validation specifically. OpenELAB's recommended validation path (bench test, then load-rig validation with independent angle measurement, then progressive vehicle testing starting at restricted speed, then mechanical inspection after each load test) implies a multi-session, iterative process, but no source quantifies total hours.
validation_strategy: Synthesized typical sequence across sources: (1) bench test the bare actuator (free-moving) to confirm basic commanded-vs-actual response; (2) loaded bench/rig test with independent steering-angle measurement - explicitly recommended because free-moving tests miss friction, compliance, and alignment errors that only appear under load (OpenELAB guidance), and this is the exact method (potentiometers at both actuator and rack, under real driving load) that surfaced the Chalmers clamp-play defect; (3) verify DT.2.2 decoupling operates correctly and is securely locked in both positions before vehicle mounting; (4) progressive vehicle testing starting at restricted speed, ramping to full autonomous-mission speeds; (5) mechanical inspection after each load test, per OpenELAB guidance, specifically to catch coupling wear/backlash before it becomes a steering-accuracy defect; (6) ongoing re-tuning from live telemetry (documented pattern: at least one team re-tuned its steering control roughly a year after first implementation, and again about a year after that).
rules_compliance_challenges: DT.2.1.1 (manual steering must be possible with the DSMS off, without other steps or actions) is the primary constraint shaping every architecture in this corpus - it rules out any design that requires the driver to manually disconnect something before regaining steering control, which is why back-drivable mechanisms (ball screws) or explicit, simple clutch/clamp mechanisms are favored over high-reduction, non-back-drivable gearing that would resist manual input even when unpowered. DT.2.2's requirement that the decoupling mechanism not have any parts removed and be securely locked in both positions rules out simple bolt-on/off actuator mounts. DT.2.1.2/DT.2.1.3 (actuation only possible when Ready-to-Drive, with a narrow, optional exception to keep steering active during an Emergency Brake Maneuver while still moving) requires the steering power supply to be gated directly off the DSMS/ASMS rather than a software-only interlock. The 2026 rules' specific belt-actuation carve-out for autonomous steering (while prohibiting belts for the primary driver steering system generally) is a rules nuance that shapes whether a belt-drive architecture is even legal to pursue.
tech_inspection_experience: [uncertain] No steering-actuator-specific tech-inspection pass/fail narrative was found in the primary sources for this item. The FSG reference guide's general steering-safety section implies inspectors will specifically verify: manual steering wheel actuation is possible whenever the DSMS is off; the steering supply is gated by the DSMS/ASMS; and (implicitly, given the DT.2.2 wording) the decoupling mechanism can be demonstrated in both positions without removing parts - these are the checks a team should expect to rehearse before tech inspection, based on rule text rather than a documented team's specific inspection story.
ebs_test_experience: See companion item 'Emergency Brake System (EBS) Design Approaches' for full detail; not the focus of this item, though note DT.2.1.3 allows the steering actuator to remain active during an Emergency Brake Maneuver while the vehicle is still moving.
documentation_burden: Less formally specified than the EBS's Pressure System Overview requirement (see companion item), but the general Engineering Design Report and Driverless Systems Form still expect the steering actuator's decoupling mechanism and power-supply gating to be documented in the same High-Level Block Diagram (DSF.4) and Actuator Power Supply Schematic (DSF.2) that cover the EBS - i.e. steering actuator documentation is folded into the same DSF package rather than requiring a separate dedicated form, which can lead teams to under-document the steering actuator relative to the EBS since it lacks its own DSF.5-equivalent section.
autonomous_speeds_achieved: N/A as team-specific results, but note: target lock-to-lock actuation times documented across the corpus cluster around 0.4-0.9 seconds (0.4 s / 2000 N documented in one rack-parallel ball-screw case; sub-0.9 s documented for AMZ's front-axle-mounted actuator), giving a common performance benchmark independent of vehicle speed.

reliability_notes: The clearest documented steering-actuator reliability issue in this corpus is Chalmers' pneumatic-clamp linear actuator: quantified 'steering reduction' (commanded angle not fully achieved) traced to play in the clamp coupling, worse on rough track surfaces, discovered via direct potentiometer comparison after a season of use. Separately, QUT's Dec 2024 crash during its EBS dynamic test (documented in the companion EBS item) was root-caused to a path-computation delay causing 'a sharp steering correction' at 40 km/h just before the finish line - a control-software timing issue interacting with the steering actuator's response, rather than a steering actuator hardware failure, but relevant as a reliability data point for the steering-control loop specifically.
top_mistakes: (1) Choosing a coupling mechanism with inherent backlash/play (a pneumatic clamp orthogonal to the column, in the one documented case) without early loaded-bench validation, only discovering the resulting steering-angle error after a full season of on-track use. (2) Sizing the actuator on PEAK torque/speed specs alone rather than continuous duty-cycle capability - explicitly warned against in current guidance ('Neither should be chosen on peak torque alone; continuous capability matters more') and consistent with every documented static-torque calculation in this corpus applying an explicit safety factor plus a separate dynamic-condition multiplier rather than trusting a single peak-spec number. (3) Trusting actuator-level encoder precision as a proxy for vehicle-level (rack/wheel) angle accuracy - current guidance explicitly warns 'An actuator encoder can be precise while the vehicle still sees error from a belt, coupling, rack joint, tire deflection, or backlash', which is precisely what happened at Chalmers even though the underlying signal chain (request vs. actuator-side readback) looked correct in isolation. (4) Skipping or shortening loaded bench testing in favor of free-moving tests, which miss the friction/compliance/alignment errors that only appear under real load (explicit current-guidance warning, consistent with the Chalmers finding that the defect was worse specifically on rougher, higher-load surfaces). (5) Descoping cost estimation as out-of-scope for the engineering design phase (documented explicitly in one thesis's own unanswered research question on cost), leaving teams with strong mechanical designs but no basis for budgeting the actual build.
advice_for_new_teams: "Start with measured tire force, axle load, and scrub radius data [not a generic torque assumption]... include thermal duty-cycle analysis, not just no-load specifications" (OpenELAB guidance, echoing the tie-rod/scrub-radius-derived torque calculations documented in the Politecnico di Torino thesis). "An actuator encoder can be precise while the vehicle still sees error from a belt, coupling, rack joint, tire deflection, or backlash" - always instrument BOTH the actuator and the rack/wheel and compare, don't trust actuator-side telemetry alone (this is literally how the Chalmers team found their clamp defect). "Device-level protection (current/temperature limits) is not a substitute for vehicle-level safety logic" (OpenELAB). "Skipping loaded bench testing: free-moving tests miss friction, compliance, and alignment errors" - budget time for a loaded rig test with independent angle measurement before vehicle mounting (OpenELAB guidance, directly consistent with what the Chalmers thesis's post-hoc testing revealed). "The cost of developing the proposed solution is not covered in this thesis" (Politecnico di Torino, 18713) - a cautionary example that mechanical design and cost/procurement planning need to be tracked as separate, explicit workstreams, since a strong mechanical design does not automatically produce a costed, buildable BOM.

recommended_sequence: (1) Derive static AND dynamic steering torque directly from tie-rod offset, scrub radius, and tire/road friction data (not a generic assumption), applying an explicit safety factor and a separate dynamic-condition multiplier. (2) Choose a transmission architecture favoring back-drivability (inline or rack-parallel ball screw, or a low-reduction QDD module) specifically to simplify DT.2.2 decoupling; only choose a higher-reduction belt/gear drive if packaging genuinely requires it, and budget extra design time for the decoupling mechanism if so. (3) Select motor/actuator on CONTINUOUS duty-cycle torque/speed capability, not peak spec. (4) Instrument BOTH the actuator and the rack/wheel with independent angle sensors from the start - do not rely on actuator-side telemetry alone. (5) Bench-test loaded, not just free-moving, comparing commanded vs. measured angle at both sensor locations, before vehicle mounting. (6) Verify the DT.2.2 decoupling mechanism is securely locked in both positions and doesn't require removing any part. (7) Progressive vehicle testing starting at restricted speed; mechanical inspection after each load test to catch coupling wear/backlash early. (8) Plan for at least one round of telemetry-driven re-tuning after initial vehicle testing, since every documented multi-year program in this corpus needed ongoing tuning well past first implementation, not a single tune-and-done cycle.
applicability_to_24_month_ramp: For a team with a running EV, ~9 software-focused members, and a 24-month window (June 2026-June 2028): the steering actuator is a comparatively contained mechanical-design problem relative to the EBS (fewer certified/regulated components, no pressure-vessel documentation burden), making it a reasonable subsystem to prioritize EARLY and potentially outsource some of the mechanical design/selection work to a COTS integrated QDD actuator module rather than designing a full custom motor+gearbox+ball-screw assembly from scratch - this trades some cost and torque/speed flexibility for a large reduction in novel mechanical engineering and procurement-lead-time risk, which suits a software-heavy team. Recommend deriving torque/speed requirements and selecting an architecture in month 1-2, targeting a bench-validated actuator (commanded-vs-actual angle confirmed under load, at both the actuator and the rack) by month 6-9, and budgeting month 9-15 for vehicle integration plus at least one telemetry-driven re-tuning pass, consistent with the corpus's demonstrated pattern of needing ongoing tuning well beyond first implementation. The single highest-leverage practice to copy from this research is instrumenting BOTH the actuator and the rack with independent angle sensors from day one, since that is precisely the method that caught the one documented in-service steering-actuator defect (Chalmers) before it became a larger problem - skipping this in favor of trusting actuator-side telemetry alone is the single most avoidable mistake identified in this research.
